title: Design a Chat App
subtitle: Route persistent connections and define delivery, ordering, presence, and group behavior
objectives: Explain why request/response can't deliver messages, and what replaces it
Design connection handling and routing when users are pinned to specific servers
Guarantee delivery and ordering without a global clock
Handle presence, group fan-out, and offline delivery at scale

exercises.title: A persistent duplex connection lets either endpoint send events
exercises.body: A WebSocket starts with an opening handshake, commonly an HTTP Upgrade, then keeps a full-duplex connection open. Either endpoint can send framed messages, so the server can push a recipient's message without waiting for that recipient to issue another request.
exercises.note: Each open connection consumes server state and file-descriptor capacity, and disconnects require explicit reconnection and catch-up behavior.

exercises.prompt: A chat client polls every five seconds for new messages. Keep one WebSocket connection open so the server can push immediately.
exercises.beforeStatus: DELIVERY DELAY · 0–5 seconds · repeated empty HTTP polls
exercises.afterStatus: DELIVERY DELAY · one network round trip on an established connection
exercises.result: Messages no longer waited for the next poll
exercises.why: A WebSocket gives the server a long-lived bidirectional connection for immediate push without repeated polling requests. The system must still track which gateway owns each connection and recover when mobile networks disconnect it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A chat client polls every five seconds for new messages. Keep one WebSocket connection open so the server can push immediately. Place Phone, Chat gateway. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Phone → Chat gateway. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A WebSocket gives the server a long-lived bidirectional connection for immediate push without repeated polling requests. The system must still track which gateway owns each connection and recover when mobile networks disconnect it.

exercises.prompt: Everything so far has been request/response: the client asks, the server answers. Why doesn't that work for chat?
choices: Because the interesting event happens on the SERVER — someone messaged you — and in request/response the server has no way to speak until you ask
exercises.why: Incoming chat messages originate independently of the recipient's requests, so the server needs a way to deliver data as soon as it arrives. A request-response-only design must repeatedly poll or hold requests open, while a persistent push channel supports server-initiated delivery.

exercises.prompt: Simplest workaround: the client polls `GET /messages` every 2 seconds. What's wrong with it?
choices: It's both too slow and too expensive: messages are up to 2 seconds late, and you pay a request per client per interval whether anything happened or not
exercises.why: Two-second polling by one million idle clients produces about 500,000 requests/sec even when no messages exist. Increasing the interval reduces load but increases delivery delay, so polling couples latency to a large volume of mostly empty requests.

exercises.prompt: Match each approach to how it works.

pairs.right: Ask, and the server holds the request open until there's news
One long-lived stream, server to client only
One connection, both directions, stays open

exercises.why: Short polling creates repeated client requests, long polling holds one request until data arrives, Server-Sent Events (SSE) maintain a server-to-client stream, and WebSocket maintains a bidirectional connection. Chat needs frequent messages in both directions, which matches WebSocket's duplex channel.

exercises.prompt: Why is WebSocket the natural fit for chat specifically?
choices: The connection stays open and either side can send at any moment — so a message pushes instantly with no request, and no per-message handshake cost
exercises.why: A WebSocket performs its connection setup once and then carries frames from either endpoint over the persistent channel. This avoids a new HTTP request for each chat event and allows the server to deliver an incoming message immediately while the connection is healthy.

exercises.prompt: You hold a WebSocket open for every online user. What have you just given up?
choices: Statelessness: that user is now bound to one specific server for as long as they're connected, so your app tier stops being interchangeable
exercises.why: A live WebSocket is attached to one server process, so that server holds connection-specific state. Horizontal scaling therefore requires routing messages to the process holding the recipient's connection and handling reconnection when that process restarts or fails.

exercises.prompt: You have 10 million users online, each holding one WebSocket. If a server can hold about 100,000 connections, roughly how many servers do you need just to hold them?
exercises.why: Ten million concurrent connections divided by 100,000 connections per server requires at least 100 servers before reserving failover or regional headroom. Connection memory, file descriptors, and heartbeat traffic therefore become primary capacity dimensions alongside message throughput.

exercises.title: A connection registry maps each online user to active connections
exercises.body: When a client connects, its gateway records a leased entry such as `user_id -> {connection_id, gateway_id}`. A user may have several entries. Delivery looks up the intended active connections, forwards the message to their gateways, and writes it to each selected socket.
exercises.note: Registry entries are ephemeral derived state; heartbeats or leases must expire entries left behind by crashes and unclean disconnects.

exercises.prompt: Bob has a live connection on Gateway 7, but Alice's message reaches Gateway 2. Route the message to the process that owns Bob's connection.
exercises.result: The message reached the machine holding Bob's live socket
exercises.why: Long-lived connections are owned by specific gateway processes. The registry maps a user or connection ID to that owner and must expire stale entries when gateways disconnect or die.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: Bob has a live connection on Gateway 7, but Alice's message reaches Gateway 2. Route the message to the process that owns Bob's connection. Place Gateway 2, Connection registry, Gateway 7. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Alice → Gateway 2; Gateway 2 → Connection registry; Gateway 2 → Gateway 7. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Long-lived connections are owned by specific gateway processes. The registry maps a user or connection ID to that owner and must expire stale entries when gateways disconnect or die.

exercises.prompt: Alice is connected to server 7. Bob is connected to server 31. Alice sends Bob a message. What's the problem?
choices: Server 7 holds Alice's connection but has no way to reach Bob's — it must discover that Bob is on server 31 and get the message there
They must be on the same server
exercises.why: Bob's socket exists on one connection server, so Alice's server cannot deliver directly without locating that process. The system needs a shared connection registry or routing layer that maps Bob's user ID to the server currently holding his connection.

exercises.prompt: Server 7 needs to know which server holds Bob's connection. Add the piece that tracks it.
exercises.why: A shared registry lets any sender resolve `user_id → connection_server` and route the message to the correct process. The mapping is ephemeral and rebuildable when clients connect, so a fast key-value store with expiration fits the access pattern.

exercises.prompt: Order the delivery of Alice's message to Bob.
steps: Alice's client sends the message over her WebSocket to server 7
One transaction stores the message and a durable delivery-stream or outbox record
A delivery worker consumes the durable record and looks up Bob's active connections
The worker routes the message to server 31, which owns Bob's socket
Server 31 pushes it down Bob's WebSocket and awaits a client acknowledgement
exercises.why: Committing the message and delivery record together closes the failure window between persistence and forwarding. If a gateway crashes after commit, another worker can consume or retry the durable record; stable message IDs let Bob's client deduplicate redelivery. Storage alone supports later history retrieval but does not trigger timely delivery.

exercises.prompt: Build durable delivery. The worker looks up Bob's gateway, then the worker—not the registry—routes the message to that gateway.
exercises.why: One transaction stores the message and pending-delivery record. A worker retries that durable work, queries the registry for Bob's current gateway, and then sends the message to that gateway; the registry returns routing data but never forwards message bytes. If Alice's gateway crashes after commit, another worker can still deliver.

exercises.prompt: Bob is offline. What happens to the message?
choices: Nothing special — it's already stored, so it simply sits there and Bob fetches it when he reconnects
It's queued in memory on server 7
exercises.why: If Bob has no live connection, the durable message remains pending in storage. On reconnection, his client requests messages after its last received cursor, which handles both ordinary offline periods and interrupted pushes through the same catch-up path.

exercises.prompt: Server 31 crashes. Bob's connection dies and he reconnects — landing on server 12. What must happen?
choices: The registry updates to say Bob is on server 12, and Bob fetches anything he missed since his last acknowledged message
The load balancer sends him back to server 31
exercises.why: After a server failure, Bob establishes a new connection and registers a new server mapping. His client supplies the last acknowledged message ID or sequence as a cursor, allowing the service to replay later durable messages without restoring the old socket.

exercises.title: A WebSocket gateway carries long-lived state for each connection
exercises.body: Ten million online users occupy ten million concurrent socket slots even when message traffic is quiet. Gateway capacity depends on file descriptors, memory, heartbeat work, and network limits; reconnect bursts require spare fleet capacity.
exercises.note: A connection registry maps each user to the gateway currently holding the socket.

exercises.prompt: Ten million users are connected. One gateway safely holds 100,000 WebSockets. Choose the *fewest* gateways that can hold every connection.
exercises.why: Ninety-nine gateways hold 9.9 million connections, leaving 100,000 without a slot. One hundred is the arithmetic minimum; failover requires spare capacity because reconnecting clients arrive as a burst.

exercises.title: Delivery state advances only when the responsible endpoint acknowledges it
exercises.body: A successful socket write usually confirms only that the local networking stack accepted the bytes; it does not prove remote receipt. A recipient-client acknowledgement confirms receipt, and a separate read acknowledgement can confirm display or consumption.
exercises.note: Lost acknowledgements cause retries, so receivers must deduplicate by message id; acknowledgements alone do not establish conversation order.

exercises.prompt: Server 31 pushes the message down Bob's socket. Is it delivered?
choices: You don't know: the write succeeded locally, but the message may still be in flight, or his phone may have lost signal before rendering it
exercises.why: A successful socket write confirms only that the server handed bytes to its network stack. Bob's client must acknowledge the message ID to prove receipt, and a separate read acknowledgement is required to prove that the conversation view displayed it.

exercises.prompt: Match each chat state to what it actually means.

pairs.right: The server accepted and stored it
The recipient's client acknowledged receiving it
The recipient's client says it was displayed
The sender's client hasn't heard back yet

exercises.why: `Sent` follows durable server acceptance, `delivered` follows an acknowledgement from the recipient device, and `read` follows an acknowledgement generated when the recipient views the message. These states can advance at different times because each depends on a different observer.

exercises.prompt: Bob's client acknowledges, but the ack is lost. What happens?
choices: The server thinks it wasn't delivered and pushes again — so Bob sees the message twice unless his client deduplicates by message id
exercises.why: If the acknowledgement is lost, the server cannot distinguish receipt from loss and must retry to preserve at-least-once delivery. The client deduplicates by stable message ID before rendering, so repeated delivery attempts produce one visible message.

exercises.prompt: Alice sends 'A' then 'B'. Bob sees 'B' then 'A'. Why can that happen?
choices: The two messages took different paths or were processed concurrently, and nothing forced them into order — network delivery has no ordering guarantee across separate operations
exercises.why: Concurrent messages can traverse different servers and queues with different delays, so arrival order does not establish send order. Reordering within one conversation can place a reply before the message it references, changing the conversation's causal meaning.

exercises.prompt: How do you order a conversation's messages without trusting anyone's clock?
choices: Partition by conversation ID and let one fenced active sequencer for that partition assign increasing conversation sequence numbers
exercises.why: Hashing conversation ID assigns each conversation to a partition whose active leader sequences its messages. On failover, a higher epoch or fencing token prevents the old owner from continuing to assign valid numbers. This avoids clock ordering and global coordination, although a very large group can become a hot conversation and may need batching or a dedicated partition.

exercises.prompt: Why is per-conversation ordering enough — why not order all messages globally?
choices: Because the product requires order within each conversation, while a global sequence would coordinate unrelated conversations without protecting an identified invariant
It would be too slow to sort
exercises.why: The stated product invariant is per-conversation order. Messages in separate conversations can be processed independently unless a specific cross-conversation feature defines another causal rule. A global counter would coordinate all writes through one sequence without protecting the requirement given here.

exercises.title: Presence is leased state distributed to interested subscribers
exercises.body: A heartbeat renews an online lease; lease expiry changes the user to offline. The presence service sends that change only to clients currently subscribed to the user's status. Each transition therefore creates fan-out proportional to the active subscriber set.
exercises.note: Debouncing disconnects and accepting a short stale interval prevent transient mobile network loss from producing repeated offline/online fan-out.

exercises.prompt: You show a green dot when a user is online. What's the naive implementation, and why does it hurt?
choices: Check the registry on each render — that's fine
Broadcasting every connect and disconnect to everyone who might care: a user with 1,000 contacts generates 1,000 notifications every time their train enters a tunnel
exercises.why: Presence changes frequently as mobile connectivity and app state fluctuate, and each change may be published to many contacts. The resulting write and fan-out load can be large even though the value becomes stale quickly and small inaccuracies are usually acceptable.

exercises.prompt: Which make presence affordable? Select all.
choices: Only compute presence for contacts the user is actually looking at right now
Debounce — wait a few seconds before declaring someone offline, so brief drops don't fan out
Accept a few seconds of staleness when the product's presence and privacy contract permits it
Store every presence change durably for audit
exercises.why: Lazy computation limits presence work to visible contacts, and debouncing suppresses rapid connect-disconnect transitions. Short expiration is appropriate only when the product contract permits bounded presence staleness; safety-sensitive or privacy controls such as hiding online status may require faster revocation. Durable auditing adds writes and storage only when that contract actually requires an audit trail.

exercises.prompt: A group chat has 100,000 members. Someone posts. What's the problem?
choices: It's fan-out again: one message must reach 100,000 connections spread across your whole server fleet, so one send becomes a storm
The group is too large to store
exercises.why: Pushing each message to every member makes write and delivery cost proportional to group size. Small groups can use eager fan-out for low latency, while very large groups can store one message and let active clients pull from a conversation cursor, avoiding work for inactive members.

exercises.prompt: You're deploying. Restarting a server drops 100,000 WebSockets at once. What happens?
choices: All 100,000 reconnect simultaneously — a thundering herd hitting your registry and catch-up reads at the same instant
exercises.why: Restarting a connection server disconnects its long-lived clients, which can create a synchronized reconnection surge. Rolling a small fraction of servers at a time and adding exponential backoff with jitter spreads connection attempts and protects registries, authentication, and gateways.

exercises.prompt: You're deciding how a mobile client gets messages while the app is backgrounded. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.leftLabel: Keep the WebSocket alive in the background
exercises.rightLabel: Drop it; use push notifications to wake the app
exercises.why: Mobile operating systems may suspend background apps and close their sockets, while frequent keepalives consume battery and radio time. Platform push services maintain shared device connectivity and wake the app for a notification, after which the app can reconnect and fetch durable messages.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the chat design.
choices: A REST API with fast polling

Persistent connections make servers stateful, so you need a registry to route to the right one, a durable store so delivery can fail safely, per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering, and client acks with dedup
A message queue between all users
exercises.why: Persistent bidirectional connections provide low-latency delivery but require a connection registry, targeted routing, and reconnection handling. Persisting messages before push makes the socket a recoverable delivery channel, while acknowledgements, deduplication, and per-conversation sequences provide delivery state and ordering.

exercises.title: Message acceptance, routing, delivery, and reading are separate transitions
exercises.body: The send API assigns a stable message ID and conversation sequence, persists the message, then publishes routing work. A connection registry locates each active recipient connection. Delivery and read states advance only from acknowledgements emitted by the endpoint responsible for that state.
exercises.note: A timeout at any transition preserves ambiguity. Retrying with the same message ID must recover the existing state instead of creating another logical message.

exercises.prompt: The send API publishes to the delivery queue, then crashes before storing the message. Bob receives an event whose message cannot be loaded later.
choices: Publish first and retry the database
Store the message and outbox event in one transaction, then relay it
Keep the message only in gateway memory
choiceFeedback: Publishing first can expose an event whose durable state never existed.
One commit makes message state and future publication recover together.
Gateway memory disappears on deploy or failure and cannot support offline delivery.
exercises.afterStatus: MESSAGE + OUTBOX COMMITTED · relay may retry safely
exercises.result: Every routable message has durable authoritative state
exercises.why: The queue and database cannot share an ordinary transaction. A transactional outbox records publication intent beside the message, so a relay can retry after crashes without routing a message that never committed or losing one that did.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: The send API publishes to the delivery queue, then crashes before storing the message. Bob receives an event whose message cannot be loaded later. Place Message + outbox, Delivery queue. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Message + outbox → Delivery queue. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The queue and database cannot share an ordinary transaction. A transactional outbox records publication intent beside the message, so a relay can retry after crashes without routing a message that never committed or losing one that did.

exercises.prompt: Build the path for a durable message to reach Bob's current WebSocket process.
exercises.why: Durable work leaves the message store through a queue. A delivery worker queries the connection registry for Bob's current connection owner, then the worker routes the message to that gateway. The registry answers a location lookup; it never forwards or persists the message.

exercises.prompt: A review finds gateway memory as the only message store, timestamps as the only ordering rule, no stable retry ID, and presence records with no expiry. Which failures follow? Select all.
choices: Clock skew can reorder one conversation
A timeout retry can create duplicate messages
Crashed clients can remain online forever
exercises.why: Each shortcut confuses transient transport state with an authoritative guarantee. Durable messages survive gateways, per-conversation sequences avoid clock ordering, stable IDs deduplicate ambiguous retries, and leases let presence expire when heartbeats stop.

exercises.prompt: A collaborative editor writes bytes to a user's WebSocket successfully, but the user's phone loses power before processing them. What has the server proved?
choices: Only that bytes were accepted by the local socket path
That the user read the update
That the message is durably synchronized
exercises.why: A successful socket write does not prove application receipt. Delivery and read states require acknowledgements from the receiving client and durable catch-up for offline devices.
